headlines.summary: Intel has been a Wall Street darling this year due to its emergence as a player in AI, but the company is being weighed down by a struggling PC market.
headlines.article_text: Intel (INTC) Q3 earnings report 2026 Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Intel issued weaker-than-expected guidance for the fourth quarter, citing ongoing softness in the PC market. "We see the PC slowdown continuing at least through the first half of next year," finance chief David Zinsner said in the earnings release. Intel shares have rocketed this year, but sold off in October as concerns emerge about the AI buildout. In this article INTC Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT Intel CEO Lip-Bu Tan speaks during a keynote presentation at Computex in Taipei on June 2, 2026. Cheng Yu-chen | AFP | Getty Images Intel shares plummeted more than 20% in extended trading on Thursday after the chipmaker issued a weak fourth-quarter forecast, citing continued softness in the global PC market. Here's how the company did in the third quarter, compared with estimates from analysts polled by LSEG: Earnings per share : 52 cents adjusted vs. 40 cents expected Revenue : $16.51 billion vs. $16.5 billion expected Revenue climbed 21% from $13.7 billion a year earlier, the company said in a press release. However, revenue in Intel's client computing and physical AI group fell 5% from the same quarter a year ago to $8.1 billion, missing estimates, even as data center and AI revenue jumped 78% to $7.3 billion. Global PC shipments declined 4% in the second quarter from a year earlier due to soaring costs for memory and other components, according to Counterpoint Research . For the current quarter, Intel said it expects adjusted earnings per share of 25 cents on revenue between $15 billion and $16 billion. Analysts were expecting revenue of $17.1 billion and EPS of 43 cents, according to LSEG. "We see the PC slowdown continuing at least through the first half of next year," Intel finance chief David Zinsner, said in the release. "We will continue making disciplined investments in capacity and working capital to increase supply and support future growth." Intel's forecast reflects the effects of an explosion at a fab in Israel that killed two workers and seriously injured a third earlier this month. The incident will cost the company about $600 million in lost revenue over two quarters, Zinsner said on Thursday's earnings. CEO Lip-Bu Tan said the explosion, which he called an "unfortunate and tragic accident," caused an "extended shutdown" at the plant, impacting shipments of 10-nanometer chips. Intel's stock has been on an upward tear, up about 150% so far this year prior to the earnings report, although it's down roughly 23% in October over growing concern over the size of the artificial intelligence buildout. "We will remain disciplined as we invest, and we will not spend $1 of capital unless we have confidence in the health of our products and process technologies, and clear evidence of customer demand," Zinsner said on the call. Nvidia , which has become the world's most valuable company thanks to its dominance in graphics processing units, or GPUs, is scheduled to report results in mid-November. Advanced Micro Devices , a maker of GPUs and central processing units, or CPUs, reports next week. Known best for its industry-leading CPUs, Intel has been a beneficiary of the rise in agentic AI. While chatbots and large models rely heavily on graphics processors from Nvidia and AMD, agentic applications such as Meta 's Muse and OpenAI's Dots lean on CPUs to help orchestrate tasks and data from a computer operating in the cloud. "Despite near term headwinds affecting the broader PC industry, we continue to see robust demand for CPUs and more broadly, for all our computing platforms in the long term," Tan said in the press release. watch now VIDEO 1:23 01:23 Intel shares plummet on lighter-than-expected Q4 guidance Closing Bell: Overtime Intel's foundry business, meanwhile, has struggled to find its footing. Intel is the only U.S.-based manufacturer of advanced logic chips, and is now in high-volume production of its most advanced 18A chip out of its new fab in Arizona, providing an alternative to Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co . Its next fab in Arizona is expected to begin operations by the end of 2028. For now, Intel has no major external customers for its new chips. "We're going to have a couple of customers ready to announce the next two quarters," Tan said on the call, adding that Intel is making "tremendous progress" on its coming 14A chips. The Trump administration took a 10% stake in Intel last year after the company had fallen behind on its 7- and 10-nanometer technologies. Nvidia and Softbank also invested billions in Intel last year. Tan has taken a more cautious approach to foundry spending than his predecessor, Pat Gelsinger, who launched an ambitious revival of the foundry business. Last week, Intel said crews have installed the first structural truss at its huge Ohio fab that was originally expected to deliver chips in 2025. In September, reports surfaced that the world's leading maker of high-bandwidth memory, SK Hynix may team up with Intel in Ohio to lease some foundry space to make memory chips at the new site. Neither company would confirm any plans. "We continue to evaluate unique and highly differentiated opportunities to accelerate our Ohio build out, and I hope to share more on this in the near future" Tan said on the call. Intel completed a $23 billion equity offering in August. Tech giants have spent trillions of dollars in recent years to meet insatiable demand for AI and the infrastructure needed to support it. Tan said he's "disappointed that we were not able to meet strong customer demand in this quarter." headlines.article_text: Microsoft announces plan to raise $25 billion in debt Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Microsoft announced the pricing for $25 billion in new debt. The company has access to the debt market but hasn't tapped it, finance chief Amy Hood told analysts on Wednesday. In this article MSFT Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT The official logo signage is pictured on the exterior facade of a Microsoft Corporation office building in Lehi, Utah, United States, on August 26, 2026. Charles-McClintock Wilson | Nurphoto | Getty Images Microsoft on Thursday announced plans to raise $25 billion in bonds, taking advantage of its healthy credit rating to support its infrastructure expansion. The software maker holds a top-tier AAA rating with S&P, a credit agency. Management is targeting $170 billion in 2026 capital expenditures, as the company looks to meet heavy demand from artificial intelligence labs Anthropic and OpenAI, as well as other clients. "Microsoft intends to use the net proceeds from the offering for general corporate purposes, which may include, among other things, funding for working capital, capital expenditures, repurchases of capital stock, acquisitions, and repayment of existing debt," according to a statement . The offerings should close on Nov. 4, the company said. Amazon and Alphabet have engaged the bond market to support infrastructure projects this year, and AI-focused cloud CoreWeave has also relied on the debt market to broaden its data center footprint. Investors have turned more skittish on companies with tall debt piles as central bankers raise interest rates to fight inflation. Microsoft will access additional funding sources to complement its own cash flow generation when conditions are attractive, Amy Hood, its finance chief, said on the company's earnings call on Wednesday. "There's a form of financing called leasing, and we've been using that one as a vehicle," she said. "We're fortunate to have access in the debt markets, given where our ratings are, and we haven't yet tapped that." Microsoft reported positive free cash flow on Wednesday, differentiating itself from Alphabet, whose cash flow was negative for the second quarter in a row. Last week Meta said it had negative free cash flow, and on Thursday Amazon reported negative free cash flow. Also on Wednesday, Oracle unveiled plans to raise $10 billion in new debt and said it anticipates a return to positive free cash flow in the second half of its 2028 fiscal year. headlines.article_text: Stocks making the biggest moves after hours: AMZN, INTC, TWLO, RDDT Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Here are some of the companies making headlines in extended trading. Amazon — Shares slid more than 6% after third-quarter results missed on the top and bottom lines. Amazon earned $1.89 per share on revenue of $201.94 billion, while analysts polled by LSEG sought $1.96 per share on $202.31 billion. The company reaffirmed its full-year guidance for capital expenditures at $220 billion. Intel — The chipmaker tanked about 21% after guidance for the current quarter came in weaker than expected. Intel sees adjusted earnings of 25 cents per share on revenue of $15 billion to $16 billion. Analysts were looking for EPS of 43 cents and $17.1 billion in revenue, per LSEG. Sandisk — The data storage device manufacturer fell 3% even after reporting an earnings and revenue beat in its fiscal first-quarter financial report. It delivered adjusted earnings of $49.51 per share compared to analysts' estimates for $46.22, per LSEG. Sandisk also announced an eight-for-one forward stock split. Starbucks — Shares were off 2% after the company reported mixed results in the fourth quarter. The company delivered revenue of $9.14 billion, compared with the $9.23 billion estimate from analysts polled by LSEG, but also posted adjusted earnings that beat expectations. Growth in the company's international business disappointed, but its domestic locations topped estimates for same-store sales growth. Pinterest – Shares dropped 8% after the company's latest quarterly results missed expectations on the top and bottom lines. For the third quarter, Pinterest earned 46 cents per share on revenue of $1.17 billion. Analysts surveyed by LSEG, however, anticipated earnings of 48 cents per share and $1.21 billion in revenue. Fourth-quarter revenue projections of $1.425 billion to $1.475 billion missed the FactSet consensus estimate of $1.52 billion. Rivian Automotive — Rivian shares added 5% after the electric-vehicle maker beat Wall Street's third-quarter expectations as it ramped up production of its new entry-level R2 SUV. Rivian reported 19,248 vehicle deliveries from July through September, up from a year earlier. The company also revised its 2026 guidance, citing expected improvements in vehicle deliveries, adjusted pretax earnings and capital expenditures. Reddit — The social media forum tanked 18% after current-quarter guidance disappointed the Street. Reddit sees fourth-quarter sales in a range of $1 billion to $1.03 billion, while the LSEG consensus estimate sought $1.05 billion. The weak outlook overshadowed top- and bottom-line beats in the third quarter. Roblox — Shares of the gaming platform shed 17% after the company gave disappointing guidance for the fourth quarter. Projected bookings for the period range from $1.89 billion to $2.00 billion, while analysts anticipated $2.00 billion. The company also guided for adjusted EBITDA losses in a range of $70 million to $10 million. Twilio — The consumer engagement platform fell 17% after the lower end of its earnings forecast fell short of estimates. Twilio sees fourth-quarter adjusted earnings of $1.48 to $1.53 per share, while analysts surveyed by LSEG expected $1.49 per share. Stryker — The maker of medical equipment slid 12% on the back of a guidance cut for the full year. The company expects adjusted earnings in a range of $14.80 to $14.90 per share, missing the FactSet consensus estimate of $14.95. Organic revenue is expected to grow at a rate of 6.5% to 7% year over year, missing analysts' forecast for an 8.2% increase. CNBC's Davis Giangiulio, Sean Conlon and Deena Zaidi contributed reporting.

headlines.title: Jim Cramer says Microsoft is winning the AI spending battle — and Alphabet is paying the price
headlines.summary: Cramer called Microsoft a buy after strong earnings, while remaining more cautious on Alphabet.
headlines.article_text: Jim Cramer on Microsoft, Alphabet AI spending Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points CNBC’s Jim Cramer said Wall Street has shifted from rewarding aggressive AI spending to favoring companies that demonstrate financial discipline and returns on their investments. Cramer said Microsoft’s strong earnings and restrained spending make it a buy, while Alphabet’s disappointing results and mounting AI costs have left him cautious on the stock. CNBC's Jim Cramer said Thursday that the market's reaction to Microsoft and Alphabet's latest earnings underscores a major shift in how Wall Street evaluates the enormous costs of the artificial intelligence boom. Investors who once rewarded tech giants for aggressively building AI infrastructure are now prioritizing financial discipline and returns on those investments. Earlier this year, Microsoft's relatively restrained spending raised concerns that it could fall behind competitors, while Alphabet was rewarded for pouring money into data centers and custom chips. But Cramer said the companies' earnings Wednesday night showed how dramatically investors' priorities have changed. "I think the stock of Microsoft, with all of its discipline, is now set to soar, while the stock of Alphabet won't rally," the " Mad Money " host said. "Too much baggage for Alphabet. No discipline. No sense of what it's supposed to be doing." Cramer's Charitable Trust , the portfolio run by CNBC's Investing Club, owns shares of both Alphabet and Microsoft. On Wednesday night, Microsoft topped earnings and revenue expectations , with revenue for its Azure cloud business growing 48% from a year earlier. Capital expenditures and finance leases of $45.2 billion also came in below Wall Street's forecasts. Cramer praised Microsoft's ability to deliver strong cloud growth while remaining free-cash-flow positive. He also highlighted the success of Copilot, its AI assistant for businesses, which "started slow, but it is becoming a screaming success." "The combination of a shrewd CEO in Satya Nadella and a tight-fisted, canny CFO in Amy Hood resulted in a quarter that will have Microsoft pull away from the crowd," Cramer said. "They run it like a business, not a science project," he added. Alphabet, meanwhile, disappointed investors. Shares plunged in Thursday's session after the Google parent missed earnings and revenue expectations , with both Search and YouTube ad revenue falling short of estimates. Although Google Cloud revenue more than doubled, that strength wasn't enough to offset concerns about its core businesses. He argued that Alphabet's massive AI investments have become harder to justify as its cash generation deteriorates. The company expects capital expenditures of $195 billion to $205 billion this year, while free cash flow turned negative for the second consecutive quarter. He also warned that Alphabet's remaining $27.6 billion in authorized stock sales could weigh on shares. "I don't want to buy more Alphabet," Cramer said. "Today was the worst day the stock ever had, but I have to wait a little bit. Let the analysts cut numbers, see where it trades, find out the right multiple." "Microsoft?
